question: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller?
title: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller
direct_answer: All four are `@Component` specializations that result in bean registration. The difference is semantic: **`@Service`** = business layer, **`@Repository`** = data layer (adds exception translation), **`@Controller`** = MVC web layer. Use the appropriate annotation to communicate intent and enable AOP targeting.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Spring stereotype annotations and their semantic meaning
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying they all do the same thing — missing @Repository's exception translation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain @Repository's persistence exception translation and why it matters

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: All four are `@Component` specializations — they all result in Spring registering the class as a bean. The differences are in semantic meaning and one concrete extra behavior. `@Service` is for your business logic layer — it communicates that this class contains business rules. `@Controller` is for MVC controllers that return views. `@RestController` combines `@Controller` and `@ResponseBody` for REST APIs. `@Repository` is for data access and has one concrete extra feature: Spring adds exception translation, which means JDBC or Hibernate exceptions are automatically translated into Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy. This makes your service layer code cleaner because you deal with one exception type instead of database-specific ones.

speakable_v2.hook: They all register a bean — but @Repository does something extra, and the others carry semantic weight that AOP and your teammates depend on.

groups.heading: @Component
groups.text: The base stereotype. Registers the class as a bean with no extra behavior. Use it for classes that don't fit the service, repository, or web layer — utilities, schedulers, event listeners.

groups.heading: @Service, @Repository, @Controller
groups.text: @Service marks business logic — semantic only. @Repository marks data access and adds exception translation: database-specific exceptions become Spring's DataAccessException. @Controller marks a Spring MVC class that returns view names. @RestController adds @ResponseBody to return JSON directly.

items: Use @Service on every class in your business logic layer — it's self-documenting and enables AOP targeting by layer.
Use @Repository on your DAO or non-JPA repository classes to get automatic exception translation.
Use @RestController on all REST API controllers — never @Controller unless you're building server-side HTML templates.
Use @Component as a fallback for infrastructure classes like schedulers, filters, and event listeners.

beats.text: non-obvious: @Repository's exception translation only applies to custom DAO classes you write with JDBC or Hibernate. Spring Data JPA repositories are interfaces — Spring Data already handles exception translation internally, so you don't need @Repository on them. But adding it doesn't hurt.

speakable_v2.cap: All four register a bean — but only @Repository adds a functional behavior. Use the right annotation for readability, AOP, and exception handling.

question: What is persistence exception translation in Spring @Repository?
title: Spring @Repository Exception Translation
direct_answer: **Persistence exception translation** means Spring converts database-specific exceptions (like `HibernateException`, `SQLException`) into its own `DataAccessException` hierarchy when thrown from a `@Repository` class. This decouples your service layer from the ORM implementation.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing what exception translation means
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why this decoupling is valuable — switch from JDBC to JPA without changing service error handling

sections.title: Why Exception Translation Matters
sections.content:
Without exception translation, a JDBC repository throws `SQLException`, a Hibernate repository throws `HibernateException`, and a JPA repository throws `PersistenceException`. Your service layer would need try-catch blocks for all these database-specific exceptions.

With `@Repository`, Spring's `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` wraps the repository in a proxy that catches these exceptions and converts them to Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy (`DataIntegrityViolationException`, `EmptyResultDataAccessException`, etc.). Service layer catches Spring exceptions only.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Without `@Repository`: service catches `HibernateException`/`SQLException` (ORM-specific)
- With `@Repository`: service catches `DataAccessException` (Spring-standard)
- `DataAccessException` is **unchecked** — no forced try-catch
- Subclasses: `DataIntegrityViolationException`, `EmptyResultDataAccessException`, etc.
- Note: with Spring Data JPA repositories, exception translation is automatic — `@Repository` is not needed on the interface

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Exception translation is the main functional benefit of `@Repository`. Without it, if your data access code throws a `HibernateException` or `SQLException`, those bubble up to your service layer and you'd have to handle ORM-specific exceptions there. `@Repository` causes Spring to wrap the class in a proxy that catches database-specific exceptions and translates them into Spring's standard `DataAccessException` hierarchy. So your service layer handles `DataIntegrityViolationException` when a unique constraint is violated, and it doesn't care whether the underlying storage is JDBC, Hibernate, or JPA. This is the classic decoupling benefit — you could swap your ORM without changing error handling in services.

followup_questions: Do Spring Data JPA repositories need @Repository?

seo.metaTitle: Spring @Repository Exception Translation | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn how Spring @Repository's persistence exception translation converts database-specific exceptions to DataAccessException for layer decoupling.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @Repository wraps your DAO in a proxy — that proxy catches every database-specific exception and re-throws it as a Spring exception your service already understands.

beats.text: Persistence exception translation is Spring's mechanism for converting ORM-specific exceptions into its own DataAccessException hierarchy. Spring's PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor detects @Repository-annotated classes and wraps them in a proxy. When the data access code throws a HibernateException, SQLException, or JPA PersistenceException, the proxy catches it and re-throws the appropriate Spring DataAccessException subclass instead.

Without translation, swapping from JDBC to JPA would mean updating every catch block in every service that handles database errors. With translation, the service always handles DataAccessException — you swap the ORM underneath and the service code doesn't know or care.

items: DataAccessException: the base class — unchecked, so you don't have to catch it if you don't need to.
DataIntegrityViolationException: thrown when a unique constraint or foreign key is violated.
EmptyResultDataAccessException: thrown when a query expects one result but finds none.
CannotAcquireLockException: thrown when a database lock can't be obtained — useful for detecting deadlocks.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, UserJdbcRepository is annotated @Repository. When saving a user with a duplicate email, the database throws a SQL unique constraint violation. Without @Repository, OrderService would catch a vendor-specific BatchUpdateException. With @Repository, the proxy converts it to DataIntegrityViolationException — a Spring type that OrderService already knows how to handle. sharp edge: Spring Data JPA repository interfaces don't need @Repository — Spring Data applies exception translation automatically for those. Adding @Repository doesn't hurt but it's redundant.

items: Exception translation only applies to classes annotated with @Repository — plain classes with database code get raw ORM exceptions.
Don't catch HibernateException or SQLException in your service layer — if you see that, it means @Repository isn't in the chain.

speakable_v2.cap: @Repository's exception translation is the one functional superpower the stereotype gives you — it keeps your service layer ORM-agnostic.

question: Can you use @Component instead of @Service or @Repository everywhere?
title: Can You Use @Component Instead of @Service @Repository?
direct_answer: **Technically yes**, `@Component` works for any bean. But you should use `@Service` and `@Repository` for proper **semantic meaning** and to benefit from `@Repository`'s exception translation. Using the correct annotation communicates layer intent and enables targeted AOP advice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands convention and best practices
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Component everywhere because it works, ignoring conventions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that AOP aspects can target specific stereotypes — @Service vs @Repository

sections.title: Why Not Just Use @Component?
sections.content:
Technically, `@Component` on `UserService` and `UserRepository` will work — both get registered as beans. But using `@Service` and `@Repository` is better for three reasons:

1. **Readability**: someone reading `@Service` immediately knows it's business logic layer
2. **`@Repository` exception translation**: only works with `@Repository`, not `@Component`
3. **AOP targeting**: you can write aspects that only apply to `@Service` beans or only to `@Repository` beans — for logging, transactions, monitoring

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `@Component` works everywhere but is the fallback for 'none of the above'
- `@Service` = business logic (semantic, no extra behavior)
- `@Repository` = data access + exception translation (functional benefit)
- `@Controller`/`@RestController` = web layer
- AOP pointcuts can target `@within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service)` — selective
- Use `@Component` for: utility classes, processors, converters that don't fit a layer

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: You can use `@Component` anywhere and it'll work — all stereotype annotations are specializations of `@Component`. But the reason to use the specific ones is a mix of convention and functionality. `@Service` clearly communicates that a class contains business logic — it's self-documenting. `@Repository` does something extra: exception translation. And for AOP, you can write advice that targets only service beans or only repository beans by checking the annotation. So the rule of thumb is: use the most specific annotation that applies. Only fall back to `@Component` for classes that don't fit neatly into web, service, or repository layers.

followup_questions: How does AOP targeting by stereotype work?

seo.metaTitle: @Component vs @Service @Repository Best Practice | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn whether you can use @Component everywhere instead of @Service and @Repository, and why using specific stereotypes is better practice.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Yes, @Component works everywhere — but that's like using a kitchen knife as a screwdriver. It fits; it's just not the right tool.

beats.text: @Component is the base stereotype — all the others are specializations of it. Technically you can annotate any class with @Component and Spring will register it as a bean. But @Service, @Repository, and @Controller exist for good reasons. They carry semantic intent and one of them — @Repository — has an extra functional behavior.

The specific stereotypes communicate architecture. When a teammate sees @Service, they immediately know the class belongs in the business layer. When they see @Component on a service class, they have to read the class to understand its role. Conventions reduce cognitive load across the whole team.

items: Readability: @Service on UserService tells every developer it's a business logic class — no guessing.
Exception translation: @Repository enables automatic DB-to-Spring exception conversion. @Component doesn't.
AOP targeting: you can write aspects that apply only to @Service beans using @within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service). @Component gets everything.
Appropriate fallback: use @Component for infrastructure classes — schedulers, filters, converters — that don't fit a named layer.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, if you annotate UserRepository with @Component instead of @Repository, it registers as a bean just fine. But when it throws a SQL constraint violation, the exception won't be translated — OrderService catches a raw vendor exception instead of DataIntegrityViolationException. non-obvious: if your team writes an AOP logging aspect targeting @within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service), it won't fire for classes annotated only with @Component — they're invisible to that pointcut.

items: Don't use @Component for every class — you lose exception translation for repositories and you make your architecture harder to read.
Don't use @Service for data access classes — the semantic mismatch confuses the next developer and disables exception translation.

speakable_v2.cap: Use the most specific annotation that fits — @Component is for anything that doesn't belong to web, service, or data access layers.

question: What does @Controller do and how is it different from @RestController?
title: @Controller vs @RestController Difference
direct_answer: **`@Controller`** marks a class as a Spring MVC controller that returns **view names** for template rendering (Thymeleaf/JSP). **`@RestController`** = `@Controller + @ResponseBody`, making every method return the response body directly as JSON/XML for REST APIs.

interviewer_intent.testing: MVC vs REST response model understanding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Controller for a REST API and forgetting @ResponseBody, getting unexpected view resolution
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @ResponseBody is the mechanism Jackson uses to serialize response

sections.title: @Controller vs @RestController
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Controller` is for the traditional Spring MVC pattern where your method returns a string view name like `'home'` and Spring renders a Thymeleaf or JSP template with that name. `@RestController` is a combination of `@Controller` and `@ResponseBody`. The `@ResponseBody` part tells Spring to take whatever your method returns and write it directly into the HTTP response body using Jackson to convert it to JSON. For any REST API backend, you always use `@RestController`. You'd use `@Controller` only if you're building a traditional server-rendered web app with templates.

followup_questions: What is @ResponseBody and what does it do?
Can you add @ResponseBody to individual methods in @Controller?
What is Spring MVC's view resolution?

seo.metaTitle: @Controller vs @RestController | Java Spring Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Understand the difference between @Controller for MVC views and @RestController for REST APIs in Spring Boot, including @ResponseBody behavior.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @RestController is just @Controller with @ResponseBody baked in — the difference is whether Spring renders a template or writes JSON.

groups.heading: @Controller
groups.text: Marks an MVC controller that handles requests and returns a view name. Spring takes the returned string — say 'home' — and renders home.html through Thymeleaf or JSP. The response is server-rendered HTML. You'd use this only if you're building a traditional web app with templates.

groups.heading: @RestController
groups.text: @Controller plus @ResponseBody combined into one annotation. @ResponseBody tells Spring to serialize the return value directly into the HTTP response body using Jackson. Instead of a view name you return a Java object, and the client receives JSON. Every method in the class gets this behavior automatically.

items: Use @RestController for every REST API endpoint — it's the standard choice for Spring Boot backends.
Use @Controller only if you're building server-side HTML with Thymeleaf or JSP — rare in modern Spring Boot APIs.

beats.text: gotcha: if you use @Controller on a REST endpoint and forget @ResponseBody, Spring tries to resolve the return value as a view name. Returning a User object causes a 404 or a template not found error because Spring looks for a view named after the object's class. Always use @RestController for JSON APIs.

speakable_v2.cap: For REST APIs, always use @RestController. Keep @Controller for template-driven web pages — it's a clear signal that the response is HTML.
followup_handoff: What is @ResponseBody and how does Jackson use it to serialize the response?

question: What is @Component in Spring and when do you use it?
title: @Component Annotation — When and How to Use It
direct_answer: **`@Component`** is the generic stereotype annotation that marks a class as a Spring-managed bean. Use it for classes that don't fit into the service, repository, or controller layers — like utility classes, event listeners, schedulers, or custom converters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of when @Component is the right choice
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Component for everything, not knowing the specific alternatives
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give specific examples: EventListener, ApplicationRunner, Converter, Filter

sections.title: When @Component Is the Right Choice
sections.content:
`@Component` is the catch-all annotation for beans that don't fit a specific layer. Common use cases:

- **`ApplicationRunner`**: runs code at startup
- **`CommandLineRunner`**: runs code at startup with command line args
- **Event listeners**: `@EventListener` methods in a `@Component`
- **Scheduled jobs**: `@Scheduled` methods in a `@Component`
- **Spring Security filters**: `OncePerRequestFilter` implementations
- **Custom converters**: implementing Spring's `Converter<S,T>` interface

sections.title: @Component Use Cases
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Component` is the most generic stereotype and you use it when none of the more specific ones apply. Good examples are startup initialization classes that implement `ApplicationRunner`, scheduled tasks with `@Scheduled` methods, custom security filters, and event listeners. These are classes that need to be Spring-managed beans so Spring can call their lifecycle methods and inject their dependencies, but they don't fit the service-repository-controller layer pattern. Anything that has a specific purpose at the infrastructure level tends to use `@Component`.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @Component and @Bean for the same class?

seo.metaTitle: @Component Annotation Spring | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn when to use @Component in Spring for utility classes, schedulers, event listeners, and infrastructure beans that don't fit service or repository layers.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @Component is the 'none of the above' stereotype — it's the right choice exactly when @Service, @Repository, and @Controller don't fit.

beats.text: @Component is the generic stereotype annotation that marks any class as a Spring-managed bean. It doesn't carry any layer semantics beyond 'this class should be managed by the container.' Spring detects it during component scanning and registers the class as a singleton bean by default.

Not every class in an application fits neatly into a business layer, data layer, or web layer. Infrastructure classes — startup hooks, schedulers, converters, filters, event listeners — need to be Spring-managed beans too. @Component is the annotation for those classes.

items: ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner: runs initialization code after the Spring context starts — @Component makes Spring discover and call it.
Scheduled jobs: a @Scheduled method must be in a Spring-managed bean — @Component handles that.
Event listeners: an @EventListener method must be in a Spring-managed bean — @Component handles that too.
Custom converters: implementing Converter<S,T> and annotating with @Component makes Spring pick it up for type conversion.
Security filters: OncePerRequestFilter subclasses are @Component beans that Spring Security wires into the filter chain.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, DataInitializer implements ApplicationRunner and is annotated @Component. After the full application context is loaded, Spring calls its run() method to seed the database. A CleanupJob class is also @Component with a @Scheduled(cron=...) method that runs at 2am daily. Neither class is a service, repository, or controller — @Component is the exact right annotation for both. non-obvious: if DataInitializer weren't a Spring bean, Spring wouldn't know to call its run() method at all.

items: Don't use @Component on service or repository classes just because it's simpler — you lose @Repository's exception translation and semantic clarity.
Don't put business logic in @Component classes — if it's business logic, it belongs in a @Service.

speakable_v2.cap: @Component is the correct choice for any infrastructure class that needs Spring management but doesn't belong to a named architectural layer.

question: How are stereotype annotations related to each other in the Spring hierarchy?
title: Spring Stereotype Annotation Hierarchy
direct_answer: All stereotype annotations are **meta-annotated with `@Component`**. `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller` all include `@Component` in their definition. `@RestController` is annotated with `@Controller`. This hierarchy means all are discovered by component scanning.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring annotation meta-annotation design
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that @Service is defined as @Component + semantic marker
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain meta-annotation concept and how Spring uses it for extensible annotation design

sections.title: The Stereotype Hierarchy
sections.content:
The annotation hierarchy:
```
@Component (base)
├── @Service   (@Component + 'service layer' marker)
├── @Repository (@Component + 'data layer' marker + exception translation)
└── @Controller (@Component + 'web layer' marker + view resolution support)
    └── @RestController (@Controller + @ResponseBody)
```

Each annotation source code includes `@Component` in its declaration:
```java
@Component  // meta-annotation — makes @Service a component
public @interface Service { ... }
```
This is **meta-annotation** — Spring checks annotations on annotations, so `@Service` is functionally recognized as `@Component`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller` are all specialized `@Component`
- Spring's component scanning uses meta-annotation detection
- `@SpringBootApplication` includes `@ComponentScan` which finds all `@Component` variants
- You can create your own stereotype: annotate your annotation with `@Component`
- `@Configuration` is also a `@Component` specialization
- Spring's `AnnotationUtils` traverses meta-annotations to find `@Component`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The stereotype annotations form a hierarchy where everything extends from `@Component`. The source code of `@Service` actually includes `@Component` in its own definition — that's called meta-annotation. Spring's component scanning doesn't just look for classes with `@Component` directly — it traverses the annotation hierarchy and finds any annotation that is itself annotated with `@Component`. This is why `@Service` classes are picked up by component scanning. This design is also how you could create your own custom stereotype annotation — annotate it with `@Component` and Spring will treat it like any other component.

followup_questions: How would you create a custom stereotype annotation?
How does Spring detect @Service as a @Component?

seo.metaTitle: Spring Stereotype Annotation Hierarchy | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Understand the Spring stereotype annotation hierarchy — how @Service, @Repository, @Controller extend @Component through meta-annotation design.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @Service's source code literally says @Component inside it — that's meta-annotation, and it's why component scanning picks up all stereotypes automatically.

beats.text: All Spring stereotype annotations are built using meta-annotation — they're annotated with @Component in their own source code. When Spring scans for beans, it doesn't just check for @Component directly. It traverses the annotation hierarchy: if a class has @Service, and @Service is itself annotated with @Component, Spring recognizes the class as a component. This is why every stereotype annotation is automatically picked up by component scanning.

Meta-annotation makes Spring's annotation system extensible. You can create your own stereotype annotation by putting @Component on it, and Spring will discover classes annotated with yours exactly as if they had @Component directly. You don't need to modify Spring's codebase.

items: @Component: the root — all other stereotypes meta-annotate with this.
@Service, @Repository, @Controller: all annotated with @Component in their source. They're just @Component plus a semantic marker.
@RestController: annotated with @Controller (which is annotated with @Component). Two levels deep.
@Configuration: also annotated with @Component — configuration classes are beans too.
Custom stereotypes: any annotation you annotate with @Component will be detected by Spring's component scanning.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan. At startup, Spring scans the package and finds UserService annotated with @Service. Spring's AnnotationUtils checks @Service and finds @Component on it. That's enough — Spring registers UserService as a bean. non-obvious: you could create @FacadeService that combines @Service and your own documentation annotation, and Spring would pick it up through the same meta-annotation chain. That's the power of this design.

items: If your custom stereotype annotation doesn't include @Component in its own meta-annotations, Spring won't detect classes annotated with it.
Don't confuse meta-annotation (annotation on annotation) with inheritance — Java annotations don't support inheritance.

speakable_v2.cap: The meta-annotation design lets Spring treat @Service, @Repository, and custom stereotypes uniformly — they're all @Component under the hood.
